claims.claim: The homily is attributed in the Patrologia Graeca to Epiphanius of Salamis, bishop of Cyprus, who lived approximately 315/320–403.

The work is catalogued as CPG 3768, titled in full 'Epiphanii episcopi Cypri oratio in divini corporis sepulturam Domini et Servatoris nostri Jesu Christi, et in Josephum qui fuit ab Arimathaea, et in Domini in infernum descensum, post salutarem passionem admirabiliter factum. Sancto et magno Sabbato.'
The homily was intended for liturgical reading on Holy Saturday (the Holy and Great Sabbath).

The homily is divided into two parts: the first praises Joseph of Arimathea for asking Pilate for Christ's body to bury it, and the second recounts the harrowing of hell, including a discourse of Jesus to Adam before Adam is released from Hades.
The Greek text was printed in Migne's Patrologia Graeca volume 43, columns 439–464, reprinting the edition of Petau (Paris, 1622).

A more modern edition of the Greek was made by Dindorf in Epiphanii episcopi Constantiae opera, Leipzig (1859–62), volume 4, part 2, pages 9–29, based on the Petau text with improvements from comparison with a 9th-century Escorial manuscript.
The text survives in numerous ancient versions including Syriac, Coptic, Armenian, Georgian, Arabic, and two different Old Slavonic versions.
